--- title: "Uneven sampling and extrapolation" description: "A model answers for conditions its survey never reached, with nothing to show that it is guessing. Past the data each method carries on in its own way, and the distance to the nearest surveyed station shows where that happens." order: 5 categories: [assumptions] --- ## Survey effort leaves conditions a model has never seen Survey effort is never spread evenly over the sea. It follows ports, weather, ship time and the questions of the day, so some conditions are sampled hundreds of times and others never. A model learns its relationships from the conditions its survey covered. Asked about anything else, it still answers, and nothing in the answer shows that it is guessing. Two problems are worth keeping apart. **Uneven sampling** means some conditions are covered thinly, so the fit there rests on a few stations. **Extrapolation** means predicting for conditions the survey did not cover at all. This page shows what three familiar methods do when they are asked to extrapolate, and how to measure how far a station lies from the survey, so that a prediction map can say where it is guessing. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Each method carries on past the data in its own shape A fitted model keeps no record of where its data stopped. Linear regression continues its straight line at the same slope. Polynomial regression follows its curve, which may turn back up wherever its bend happens to fall. A decision tree sends every value beyond its last split to the same leaf as the most extreme stations it saw, so a random forest, an average of such trees, repeats the value at the edge. Its predictions are never absurd, which makes them easy to trust, but they stay flat however far the truth moves on. ::: {.diagram} ![Three methods fitted to the same data and asked about values beyond it. Linear regression continues at the same slope, polynomial regression follows its own bend, and a random forest repeats the value at the edge of the data. None of them shows that it has left the data.](img/past-the-data.svg){fig-alt="Three cards, each with the same points falling across the left part of a small chart, a shaded region on the right marked beyond the data, and a dashed true curve that keeps falling gently towards zero. Linear regression: a straight line carries on at the same slope into the shaded region and drops below zero. Polynomial regression: a curve follows the points and turns back upward past the data. Random forest: a stepped line follows the points and runs flat across the shaded region at the value of the last points. A note says none of them shows that it has left the data."} ::: ## Worked example The survey here visits only the shallower sites: those whose stations average less than 100 m deep. The deeper sites are the area the model is asked to map. Three methods from earlier pages are fitted with the same inputs: polynomial regression from [Linear and polynomial regression](../03-supervised-learning/linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd) and the negative binomial model from [Distributional assumptions](distributional-assumptions.qmd), both with squared terms for depth and temperature, and the random forest from [Forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd). One survey could be lucky or unlucky, so the fit is repeated on ten surveys, each made of a different three quarters of the shallow sites. The quarter left out each time gives new sites within the survey's depths, to set against the deep sites. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() |> mutate(site_depth = mean(depth_m, na.rm = TRUE), .by = site_id) shallow <- filter(survey, site_depth < 100) deep <- filter(survey, site_depth >= 100) # ten surveys, each of three quarters of the shallow sites surveys <- group_mc_cv(shallow, group = site_id, prop = 0.75, times = 10) forest_recipe <- recipe( abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season, data = shallow ) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_relevel(substrate, ref_level = "sand") curve_recipe <- forest_recipe |> step_poly(depth_m, temperature_c, degree = 2, options = list(raw = TRUE)) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import statsmodels.api as sm from scipy.spatial.distance import cdist from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import (OneHotEncoder, PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler) from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean, load_coastal_survey_truth survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() survey["site_depth"] = survey.groupby("site_id")["depth_m"].transform("mean") shallow = survey[survey["site_depth"] < 100].reset_index(drop=True) deep = survey[survey["site_depth"] >= 100].reset_index(drop=True) # ten surveys, each of three quarters of the shallow sites surveys = list(GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=10, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) .split(shallow, groups=shallow["site_id"])) categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] + categorical def squared(column): return (column, Pipeline([ ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("poly", PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False)), ]), [column]) curve_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ squared("depth_m"), squared("temperature_c"), ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), ["chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"]), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(drop=["sand", "spring"], sparse_output=False), categorical), ]) forest_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), predictors[:4]), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), categorical), ]) ``` ::: ::: The survey has 97 of the 160 sites. The other 63 sites, down to 195 m, are the area to map. ### The three methods part company below the survey's depths Each of the ten surveys fits all three methods, which then predict every station at the left-out shallow sites and at the deep sites. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} predict_three <- \(one_survey) { fitting <- analysis(one_survey) new_sites <- bind_rows(assessment(one_survey), deep) polynomial <- fit(workflow(curve_recipe, linear_reg()), fitting) prepped <- prep(curve_recipe, training = fitting) nb_fit <- MASS::glm.nb(abundance ~ ., data = bake(prepped, new_data = NULL)) forest <- fit( workflow(forest_recipe, rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("regression")), fitting ) new_sites |> select(station_id, site_id, depth_m) |> mutate( "Polynomial regression" = predict(polynomial, new_sites)$.pred, "Negative binomial model" = predict(nb_fit, bake(prepped, new_sites), type = "response"), "Random forest" = predict(forest, new_sites)$.pred ) } predictions <- surveys |> mutate(predicted = map(splits, predict_three)) |> select(id, predicted) |> unnest(predicted) |> pivot_longer(c("Polynomial regression", "Negative binomial model", "Random forest"), names_to = "model", values_to = "predicted") ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} def predict_three(fit_rows, held_rows): fitting = shallow.iloc[fit_rows] new_sites = pd.concat([shallow.iloc[held_rows], deep], ignore_index=True) polynomial = Pipeline([("recipe", curve_recipe), ("model", LinearRegression())]).fit( fitting[predictors], fitting["abundance"]) prepped = curve_recipe.fit(fitting[predictors]) design = sm.add_constant(prepped.transform(fitting[predictors])) nb_fit = sm.NegativeBinomial(fitting["abundance"].to_numpy(), design).fit( method="newton", disp=0) forest = Pipeline([ ("recipe", forest_recipe), ("model", RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, random_state=1, n_jobs=-1)), ]).fit(fitting[predictors], fitting["abundance"]) new_design = sm.add_constant(prepped.transform(new_sites[predictors]), has_constant="add") return new_sites[["station_id", "site_id", "depth_m"]].assign( **{"Polynomial regression": polynomial.predict(new_sites[predictors]), "Negative binomial model": nb_fit.predict(new_design), "Random forest": forest.predict(new_sites[predictors])}) predictions = pd.concat( [predict_three(fit_rows, held_rows).assign(id=i) for i, (fit_rows, held_rows) in enumerate(surveys)] ).melt(id_vars=["id", "station_id", "site_id", "depth_m"], var_name="model", value_name="predicted") ``` ::: ::: The survey is simulated, so the predictions can be compared with the **true mean count** at each station: the number the simulation drew that station's count around, before the chance of the catch was added. No real study has this, and no score computed against it could be achieved in practice. It is used here because it shows each method's error free of the noise in single counts. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} predictions <- predictions |> left_join(load_coastal_survey_truth(), by = "station_id") ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} predictions = predictions.merge(load_coastal_survey_truth(), on="station_id") ``` ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bands <- predictions |> filter(between(depth_m, 20, 180)) |> mutate(depth = 20 * floor(depth_m / 20) + 10) truth_line <- bands |> summarise(true_mean = mean(true_mean), .by = c(model, depth)) bands |> summarise(predicted = mean(predicted), .by = c(model, id, depth)) |> ggplot(aes(depth, predicted)) + annotate("rect", xmin = 100, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey92") + geom_line(aes(group = id), colour = ml_palette[["blue"]], alpha = 0.45) + geom_line(aes(y = true_mean), data = truth_line, linewidth = 1.3) + facet_wrap(~ fct_relevel(model, "Polynomial regression", "Negative binomial model")) + labs(x = "Depth (m)", y = "Mean count (individuals)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Mean predicted count at new sites in 20 m bands of depth, one thin line for each of the ten shallow surveys, against the true mean count (black). The shaded region holds the depths of the sites the surveys left out. Within the survey's depths the ten fits of each method agree with each other and with the truth. Below them the random forest's lines run flat, and the two curves' lines fan out.](sampling-and-extrapolation_files/figure-html/fig-beyond-1.png){#fig-beyond fig-alt='Three panels, one per method, each with depth from 20 to 180 metres on the horizontal axis and mean count on the vertical, with the region deeper than 100 metres shaded. A thick black line for the true mean count falls from about 7 at 30 metres to about 4 at 90 metres, stays near 3.5 to 120 metres and then drops to about 1 at 170 metres. In every panel the ten thin blue lines bunch around the black line up to 100 metres. Beyond it: for polynomial regression and the negative binomial model the thin lines spread out, some following the black line down, others staying level or turning upward; for the random forest all ten lines stay level between about 3 and 5, well above the black line at the deepest bands.' width=1700} ::: ::: ::: Within the survey's depths, @fig-beyond shows the ten fits of each method bunched around the truth. Past 100 m they part company. The random forest's lines run flat: it predicts a station at 170 m much as it predicts one at the deepest point of its survey, while the true mean count keeps falling. The lines of polynomial regression and the negative binomial model fan out instead: some fits follow the truth down, others level off or turn back up. ### The forest is too high on every survey and the curves only on some For each survey, each method's mean prediction is divided by the mean true count, once over the left-out shallow sites and once over the stations deeper than 140 m, where the true mean count averages 1.8. A ratio of 1 is right on average; 2 is twice too high. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ratios |> summarise(lowest = min(ratio), highest = max(ratio), .by = c(model, where)) |> mutate(range = paste(format(round(lowest, 1), nsmall = 1), format(round(highest, 1), nsmall = 1), sep = "–")) |> select(model, where, range) |> pivot_wider(names_from = where, values_from = range) |> rename(Method = model, "Left-out shallow sites" = within, "Stations deeper than 140 m" = below) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Method |Left-out shallow sites |Stations deeper than 140 m | |:-----------------------|:----------------------|:--------------------------| |Polynomial regression |0.8–1.2 |0.7–3.7 | |Negative binomial model |0.8–1.2 |1.1–3.7 | |Random forest |0.8–1.2 |1.8–2.8 |
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} predictions["where"] = np.select( [predictions["site_id"].isin(shallow["site_id"]), predictions["depth_m"] > 140], ["Left-out shallow sites", "Stations deeper than 140 m"], default="") ratios = (predictions[predictions["where"] != ""] .groupby(["model", "id", "where"])[["predicted", "true_mean"]].mean() .eval("ratio = predicted / true_mean") .groupby(["model", "where"])["ratio"].agg(["min", "max"]).round(1)) ratios["range"] = ratios["min"].astype(str) + "–" + ratios["max"].astype(str) ratios["range"].unstack().reset_index(names="Method") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | Method | Left-out shallow sites | Stations deeper than 140 m | |:------------------------|:-------------------------|:-----------------------------| | Negative binomial model | 0.8–1.3 | 1.3–4.2 | | Polynomial regression | 0.8–1.2 | 1.1–3.6 | | Random forest | 0.9–1.2 | 2.2–3.5 | ::: ::: ::: At the left-out shallow sites every method is close to right on every survey, with ratios between 0.8 and 1.2. Below 140 m the random forest is too high on all ten surveys, at 1.8 to 2.8 times the truth. Polynomial regression ranges from 0.7 to 3.7 and the negative binomial model from 1.1 to 3.7: a curve can be close to right or far off, depending on which sites its survey happened to include. The survey is simulated, so the reason can be given. The simulation makes the species' numbers rise with depth to a peak at 80 m and fall beyond it, a curve on the log scale of just the shape that the negative binomial model's squared terms draw. Even so, its fits fan out. Within 100 m the water gets colder as it gets deeper, so the depth curve and the temperature curve can trade off against each other, and fits that describe the shallow sites equally well can bend in different directions below them. A better fit within the data is not a more correct model, as [Linearity and nonlinearity](linearity-and-nonlinearity.qmd) found for the GAM, and past the data the difference shows. ## A range check misses new combinations of conditions Spotting that 170 m lies beyond a survey of sites shallower than 100 m is easy. The harder case is a station inside the survey's range of every input, taken one at a time, in a combination of conditions the survey never met. Suppose a survey sailed only in summer and autumn, and its model is asked about spring and winter stations. The usual check takes each input in turn and asks whether a station's value lies between the smallest and largest the survey recorded. A check that looks at all the inputs together measures the **distance to the nearest surveyed station**. Each input is first put on a common scale, standardised to a mean of 0 and a spread of 1 as in [Scaling and encoding](../02-marine-data/scaling-and-encoding.qmd), with chlorophyll logged first. The distance is then the straight-line distance across depth, temperature, chlorophyll and salinity together. A distance means little alone, so it is compared with how far surveyed stations lie from their own nearest neighbour at another site. A station further from the survey than 95% of surveyed stations are from their neighbours is flagged as far from the survey. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} surveyed <- filter(survey, season %in% c("summer", "autumn")) asked <- filter(survey, season %in% c("spring", "winter")) inputs <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu") distance_recipe <- recipe(surveyed[inputs]) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric()) |> step_log(chlorophyll_mg_m3) |> step_normalize(all_numeric()) |> prep() surveyed_scaled <- as.matrix(bake(distance_recipe, new_data = NULL)) asked_scaled <- as.matrix(bake(distance_recipe, asked)) # distance from each row of `from` to the nearest row of `to` nearest <- \(from, to) { apply(from, 1, \(row) min(sqrt(colSums((t(to) - row)^2)))) } # how far each surveyed station lies from the nearest at another site neighbour_gap <- map_dbl(seq_len(nrow(surveyed)), \(i) { other_sites <- surveyed$site_id != surveyed$site_id[i] nearest(surveyed_scaled[i, , drop = FALSE], surveyed_scaled[other_sites, ]) }) limit <- quantile(neighbour_gap, 0.95) in_range <- \(column) { seen <- range(surveyed[[column]], na.rm = TRUE) is.na(asked[[column]]) | between(asked[[column]], seen[1], seen[2]) } asked <- asked |> mutate(distance = nearest(asked_scaled, surveyed_scaled), far = distance > limit, every_range = reduce(map(inputs, in_range), `&`)) asked |> summarise(stations = n(), `inside every range` = sum(every_range), `far from the survey` = sum(far), `inside every range but far` = sum(every_range & far)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| stations| inside every range| far from the survey| inside every range but far| |--------:|------------------:|-------------------:|--------------------------:| | 406| 279| 243| 132|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} surveyed = survey[survey["season"].isin(["summer", "autumn"])].reset_index(drop=True) asked = survey[survey["season"].isin(["spring", "winter"])].reset_index(drop=True) inputs = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] def logged(frame): return frame[inputs].assign( chlorophyll_mg_m3=np.log(frame["chlorophyll_mg_m3"])) distance_recipe = Pipeline([ ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler()), ]).fit(logged(surveyed)) surveyed_scaled = distance_recipe.transform(logged(surveyed)) asked_scaled = distance_recipe.transform(logged(asked)) # how far each surveyed station lies from the nearest at another site gaps = cdist(surveyed_scaled, surveyed_scaled) same_site = surveyed["site_id"].to_numpy()[:, None] == surveyed["site_id"].to_numpy() gaps[same_site] = np.inf limit = np.quantile(gaps.min(axis=1), 0.95) def in_range(column): low, high = surveyed[column].min(), surveyed[column].max() return asked[column].isna() | asked[column].between(low, high) asked["distance"] = cdist(asked_scaled, surveyed_scaled).min(axis=1) asked["far"] = asked["distance"] > limit asked["every_range"] = np.logical_and.reduce([in_range(c) for c in inputs]) pd.DataFrame({ "stations": [len(asked)], "inside every range": [asked["every_range"].sum()], "far from the survey": [asked["far"].sum()], "inside every range but far": [(asked["every_range"] & asked["far"]).sum()], }) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | stations | inside every range | far from the survey | inside every range but far | |-----------:|---------------------:|----------------------:|-----------------------------:| | 406 | 279 | 243 | 132 | ::: ::: ::: Of the 406 spring and winter stations, 279 pass the range check on every input. Yet 132 of those, 47% of the stations that pass, are far from every surveyed station, and 97 of those are winter stations. @fig-novelty shows why. In summer and autumn shallow water is warm, so the survey met cold water only at depth. Winter cools the shallow water to temperatures the survey recorded, at depths it covered, but never together. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} novelty <- asked |> mutate(status = case_when( !every_range ~ "Outside a range", far ~ "Inside every range, far from the survey", .default = "Close to surveyed stations" )) ggplot(mapping = aes(depth_m, temperature_c)) + annotate("rect", xmin = min(surveyed$depth_m, na.rm = TRUE), xmax = max(surveyed$depth_m, na.rm = TRUE), ymin = min(surveyed$temperature_c, na.rm = TRUE), ymax = max(surveyed$temperature_c, na.rm = TRUE), fill = NA, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], linetype = "dashed") + geom_point(data = surveyed, colour = "grey75", size = 1.2) + geom_point(aes(colour = status), data = novelty, size = 1.6, alpha = 0.85) + scale_colour_manual(values = c( "Close to surveyed stations" = ml_palette[["sky"]], "Outside a range" = ml_palette[["blue"]], "Inside every range, far from the survey" = ml_palette[["orange"]] )) + guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 1)) + labs(x = "Depth (m)", y = "Temperature (°C)", colour = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Depth against temperature for the summer and autumn survey (grey) and the spring and winter stations its model is asked about. The dashed box is the survey's range of each input taken alone. Orange stations are inside every range yet far from any surveyed station; most are shallow and cold, a combination the survey did not meet, as its cold water was all deep.](sampling-and-extrapolation_files/figure-html/fig-novelty-1.png){#fig-novelty fig-alt='A scatter plot with depth from 0 to 200 metres on the horizontal axis and temperature from about 2 to 16 degrees on the vertical. Grey points, the summer and autumn survey, form a band that cools with depth, from about 10 to 16 degrees in shallow water to 6 to 11 degrees at 150 metres. A dashed box marks the survey\'s range of depth and temperature. Spring and winter stations are coloured: light blue ones, close to surveyed stations, sit along the lower edge of the grey band; dark blue ones, outside a range, lie mostly below the box, colder than any surveyed station, at depths beyond 90 metres; orange ones, inside every range but far from the survey, form a band beneath the grey points between the surface and about 100 metres, at 5 to 8 degrees, where the survey has no stations.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: ### The forest's error grows with distance from the survey A random forest fitted to the summer and autumn survey predicts the spring and winter stations. Season itself is left out of its inputs, as the survey has none of the seasons asked about. Its predictions are compared with the true mean count again, which only a simulation allows, in four groups of stations from the nearest quarter to the furthest. A prediction 2 times too high or 2 times too low is off by a factor of 2. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} season_forest <- workflow( recipe(abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate, data = surveyed) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()), rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("regression") ) |> fit(surveyed) by_distance <- asked |> mutate(predicted = predict(season_forest, asked)$.pred) |> left_join(load_coastal_survey_truth(), by = "station_id") |> mutate(quarter = ntile(distance, 4), off_by = exp(abs(log(predicted / true_mean)))) |> summarise(stations = n(), `distance from` = min(distance), to = max(distance), `typical factor off` = median(off_by), .by = quarter) |> arrange(quarter) by_distance |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| quarter| stations| distance from| to| typical factor off| |-------:|--------:|-------------:|----:|------------------:| | 1| 102| 0.12| 0.62| 1.37| | 2| 102| 0.63| 0.99| 1.73| | 3| 101| 1.00| 1.35| 2.20| | 4| 101| 1.35| 3.29| 2.69|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} season_inputs = inputs + ["substrate"] season_forest = Pipeline([ ("recipe", ColumnTransformer([ ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), inputs), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), ["substrate"]), ])), ("model", RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, random_state=1, n_jobs=-1)), ]).fit(surveyed[season_inputs], surveyed["abundance"]) by_distance = asked.assign( predicted=season_forest.predict(asked[season_inputs]) ).merge(load_coastal_survey_truth(), on="station_id") by_distance["quarter"] = pd.qcut(by_distance["distance"], 4, labels=[1, 2, 3, 4]) by_distance["off_by"] = np.exp(np.abs(np.log(by_distance["predicted"] / by_distance["true_mean"]))) (by_distance.groupby("quarter", observed=True) .agg(stations=("distance", "size"), distance_from=("distance", "min"), to=("distance", "max"), typical_factor_off=("off_by", "median")) .round(2).reset_index()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | quarter | stations | distance_from | to | typical_factor_off | |----------:|-----------:|----------------:|-----:|---------------------:| | 1 | 102 | 0.12 | 0.62 | 1.39 | | 2 | 101 | 0.63 | 0.99 | 1.87 | | 3 | 101 | 0.99 | 1.34 | 2.32 | | 4 | 102 | 1.35 | 3.3 | 3.15 | ::: ::: ::: At the quarter of stations nearest the survey, the forest is typically off by a factor of 1.4. At the furthest quarter it is typically off by 2.7. The forest reports nothing different at the far stations; the distance is the only sign that its predictions there deserve less trust. ## A prediction map needs its distance from the survey The distance to the nearest surveyed station can be mapped alongside any prediction, so that a reader sees where the map rests on the survey and where it is extrapolating. Areas far from the survey can be greyed out or left unmapped. The same distance shows uneven sampling too: conditions the survey covered thinly sit further from their nearest station than well-covered ones, and their predictions rest on fewer stations. Sometimes extrapolating is the point, as in projecting a species' range under warmer water than any survey recorded. Then say plainly which predictions are extrapolations, prefer a model whose shape can be defended from what is known about the species, and expect errors larger than any cross-validation on the survey has measured. Spatial blocks, from [Spatial and temporal dependence](spatial-and-temporal-dependence.qmd), measure part of this, as a held-out block often holds conditions the rest of the map covers thinly. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A model answers for conditions its survey never covered, and nothing in its predictions shows that it has left the data. - Past the data, a random forest repeats the value at the edge. Below 140 m it was too high on all ten shallow surveys, at 1.8 to 2.8 times the true mean count. - Polynomial regression and the negative binomial model follow their curves, which can be close to right or far off depending on the survey: from 0.7 to 3.7 and 1.1 to 3.7 times the truth. - A range check on each input misses new combinations. 132 of the 279 spring and winter stations that passed it were far from every surveyed station. - The distance to the nearest surveyed station, on standardised inputs, flags such stations. The forest's typical error grew from a factor of 1.4 at the nearest quarter of stations to 2.7 at the furthest. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Refit the forest in `predict_three()` with `rand_forest(trees = 500, min_n = 50)`, so each leaf holds at least 50 stations, and redraw @fig-beyond. Does a smoother forest extrapolate any better? 2. Use `nearest()` to measure how far each deep station lies from the shallow survey, with both sets of stations prepared by a `distance_recipe` built on `shallow`. Do the stations deeper than 140 m stand out?
